Gerontological nursing · Unfolding case exam

Marcus Reyes, 72: Heart Failure, Kidney Failure, Hyperkalemia & Transitions in Late Life

Read the case background, then work through the case in six parts. Each part opens when you finish the one before it. At eight key decisions, your choice changes what happens next before the case returns to the main path. All 85 multiple-choice questions are worth 1 point each.

PatientMarcus Reyes
Age / sex72 / male
BackgroundVietnam veteran
Estimated dry weight65 kg
Health care agentElena (daughter)
CourseHospital Days 1–6; skilled nursing facility Days 7–8

Case background

Marcus is a 72-year-old veteran with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF), a left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) of 25%, chronic kidney disease (CKD), atrial fibrillation on warfarin, type 2 diabetes, and bipolar disorder treated for years with lithium. Over several days at home he became confused, short of breath, weak, and nauseated, and he fell. A recent course of naproxen for gout had caused fluid retention, and an urgent care visit doubled his diuretic instead of stopping the nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID), a prescribing cascade. Several prescribers, an auto-refill, and a pill box kept overlapping drugs going.

He arrives with acute kidney injury (AKI) on chronic kidney disease, severe hyperkalemia with electrocardiogram (ECG) changes, pulmonary edema, lithium and digoxin toxicity, hypoglycemia, and delirium. The case follows him through emergency dialysis, a hospital stay with complications, and transfer to a skilled nursing facility, while his family copes with caregiving strain, a dying brother, and suspected mistreatment of his wife at home.

Active problems on admission

Hyperkalemia, potassium 7.1 mEq/L Acute kidney injury on chronic kidney disease; estimated glomerular filtration rate 17 Lithium toxicity Digoxin toxicity Delirium Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, stage C Pulmonary edema Metabolic acidosis Hypoglycemia Atrial fibrillation Gout flare Osteoarthritis Diabetic neuropathy Glaucoma, cataracts Hearing loss Depression, posttraumatic stress disorder Hazardous drinking Fall before admission

Brown-bag medications from home

  • Heart and kidney: spironolactone, sacubitril/valsartan and lisinopril, furosemide, carvedilol, digoxin 0.25 mg, potassium chloride, a potassium salt substitute
  • Other prescriptions: lithium, glyburide, warfarin, timolol eye drops, oxybutynin, zolpidem
  • Over the counter: naproxen, aspirin, diphenhydramine, ginkgo biloba, heavy alcohol use

Creatinine / creatinine clearance3.6 mg/dL / ≈ 17 mL/minUsual creatinine 1.8; every drug cleared by the kidneys accumulates
Blood urea nitrogen98 mg/dLUremia with confusion and a pericardial rub
Arterial blood gas (room air)pH 7.28 / 30 / 16 / 58pH, carbon dioxide, bicarbonate, and oxygen values showing metabolic acidosis with low oxygen from pulmonary edema
Lithium level1.6 mEq/LToxic, with confusion and tremor; removed by dialysis
Digoxin level2.6 ng/mLToxic, with a slow heart rate, nausea, and yellow vision; not removed by dialysis
Glucose58 mg/dLGlyburide in kidney failure, with warning signs masked by beta blockers
Calcium / phosphorus / parathyroid hormone7.9 / 6.9 / 312Mineral and bone disorder of chronic kidney disease
Hemoglobin9.1 g/dLAnemia of chronic kidney disease (low erythropoietin)
Corrected QT interval≈ 490 msProlonged by low calcium and lithium; drugs that prolong it further are dangerous
Blood pressure / respiratory rate96/58 / 28Low-normal blood pressure; rapid breathing compensating for acidosis
EchocardiogramEjection fraction 25%Dilated left ventricle, eccentric hypertrophy, functional mitral regurgitation

Hospital and skilled nursing facility course

Day 1

Admitted. Ten unsafe admission orders must be questioned, including drugs that raise potassium, lithium, digoxin 0.25 mg, glyburide, meperidine, as-needed intramuscular haloperidol, as-needed restraints with full side rails, and a urinary catheter for measuring intake and output. Meets all five urgent dialysis indications (Acidosis, Electrolytes, Intoxication, Overload, Uremia) and receives urgent hemodialysis.

Day 2

Delirium confirmed with the Confusion Assessment Method at 0200, with hypervigilance. Refuses sevelamer because the pills are too big. Geriatric assessment: all six Fulmer SPICES problems are present (Sleep disorders, Problems with eating or feeding, Incontinence, Confusion, Evidence of falls, Skin breakdown). Pain Assessment in Advanced Dementia score of 6 during a gout flare.

Day 3

Hypoactive delirium in the afternoon. Stable enough to begin phase I cardiac rehabilitation.

Day 4

Heart rate 48 with dizziness; digoxin and timolol held. Coughing after thin liquids, new right lower lobe consolidation, white blood cell count 13.1: likely aspiration pneumonia. Blood pressure falls to 84/50 during dialysis. Braden score 11 with a stage 2 sacral pressure injury.

Day 5

Now below dry weight: orthostatic hypotension and dark, low urine output. Atrial fibrillation with a rapid ventricular response. Fecal impaction. Geriatric Depression Scale (15-item) score of 10, a loaded revolver at home, and statements about being a burden. Signs of financial exploitation and abuse of Rosa at home.

Day 6

Lightheaded with a blood pressure drop during cardiac rehabilitation soon after a dialysis run. Discharge planning: long-term dialysis, access care, transitions, and legal and financial questions.

Day 7–8

Transferred to sub-acute care at a skilled nursing facility with outpatient dialysis. Resident rights questions, and differential reasoning about other residents' presentations.

Family and social context

  • Rosa, his wife, has Parkinson's disease and can no longer cook. Marcus wants to go home to care for her.
  • Elena, his daughter, is his agent under a durable power of attorney for health care. She is exhausted and drinking more.
  • Daniel, his son, holds a general financial power of attorney, buys processed food, and has $14,200 in unexplained withdrawals.
  • Tomás, his brother, is dying in hospice. Gerald is family in all but law, and his grief may go unrecognized.
  • Money is short. He has Medicare and a Medigap plan and may qualify for Department of Veterans Affairs benefits.

Frameworks you will apply

  • American Geriatrics Society Beers Criteria (2023), kidney-based drug dosing by the Cockcroft-Gault formula, and deprescribing
  • Confusion Assessment Method; Fulmer SPICES; Geriatric Depression Scale (15-item); Mini Nutritional Assessment–Short Form; Braden Scale; Morse Fall Scale; Pain Assessment in Advanced Dementia; Alcohol Use Disorders Identification Test–Consumption
  • Situation-Background-Assessment-Recommendation (SBAR) communication; the LEARN model (Listen, Explain, Acknowledge, Recommend, Negotiate); the PLISSIT model (Permission, Limited Information, Specific Suggestions, Intensive Therapy); the 5 Ls of firearm safety; the Progressively Lowered Stress Threshold model
  • Hyperkalemia treatment: stabilize, shift, remove
  • Urgent dialysis indications (Acidosis, Electrolytes, Intoxication, Overload, Uremia); intermittent hemodialysis, continuous renal replacement therapy modes, and peritoneal dialysis
  • Restraint-free care, prevention of catheter-associated urinary tract infection, and transitional care
  • Palliative care, hospice, and advance care planning
Thread to follow

Most of Marcus's crisis was preventable. Ask of every finding: is this a drug effect, an atypical presentation of acute illness, or a reversible cause, before attributing it to age?
